                                               1. Introduction

   If we are to compute operations on numbers (which could be integers, real numbers,
Gaussian integers, complex numbers, or even p-adic numbers), we first need to agree on a
way to represent these numbers. The theory of numeration systems examines the different
methods that can be used to represent numbers through sequences of symbols. Depending
on the tasks we are interested in performing, we can then try to select the most suitable
numeration system. A desirable property of the chosen system is that the operations of
interest can be performed by some finite state machine.

   In this paper, we consider the representation of non-negative integers via positional nu-
meration systems as initiated by Fraenkel [19]. As explained in the nice chapter by Frougny
and Sakarovitch [21], perhaps the most fundamental question to be asked is to understand
which positional numeration systems support a regular set of representations. That is, do
all valid expansions form a regular language in the sense of finite automata? Indeed, the
regularity of the set of expansions is a necessary condition to the use of automata-theoretic
techniques in relation to numeration systems. We can mention the ability to normalize
representations with transducers [20, 22], which enables the computation of addition in the
numeration system using finite state machines. In turn, this allows us to use tools such as
Walnut[29, 36] to automatically prove results related to the numeration system, following
a connection to first-order logic pioneered by Büchi [9].

   Most of the commonly used numeration systems, even in the non-standard numeration
systems community, have the property to generate a regular numeration language. This is
the case of all Bertrand numeration systems associated with a Parry number. These define
a very constrained family of positional numeration systems since there are only one or two
Bertrand numeration systems associated with a given Parry number [7, 15]. All integer
base systems as well as the Zeckendorf numeration system [37] based on the Fibonacci
sequence are Bertrand numeration systems. Another family with this property is that
of Pisot numeration systems, which are the positional numeration systems defined by a
linear recurrence relation whose characteristic polynomial is the minimal polynomial of a
Pisot number [22, 8]. This time, many Pisot numeration systems are associated with one
given Pisot number, since the initial conditions can be more freely chosen. Nevertheless,
this family is still very special, in particular because of the irreducibility constraint on the
characteristic polynomial. These two families share the property of having a dominant root,
meaning that the quotient of consecutive terms in the base sequence admits a limit, which
in addition is greater than one. On the other hand, even some simple numeration systems,
like the one based on the sequence of squares, do not support a regular set of representations
[35].

   As an attempt to unify the theory of numeration systems with a regular numeration
language, Lecomte and Rigo defined the family of abstract numeration systems [25, 26].
Here, the point of view is reversed. One starts with any given regular language, orders the
words in the language with respect to the radix order (i.e., by length first and then using
the lexicographic order within each length) and declares that a non-negative integer n is
represented by the n-th word in the language. This framework encompasses the previously
mentioned families of numeration systems as well as others, such as the Dumont-Thomas
numeration systems built from a substitution [17]. The price of this very general point of
view is that we lose the information of the algorithm to directly produce the representation
NUMERATION SYSTEMS WITHOUT A DOMINANT ROOT AND REGULARITY  3

of a number. This raises the question of determining which regular languages can be
produced by a positional numeration system. This problem was studied in [24] for the
family of Dumont-Thomas numeration systems.

   The question of characterizing positional systems generating a regular numeration lan-
guage was addressed by Hollander in the case where the numeration system satisfies the
dominant root condition [23]. In his study, Hollander provided a detailed, however not full,
description of systems with a dominant root and giving rise to a regular set of representa-
tions. In particular, he does not entirely solves the issue of the dependence to the initial
conditions. Central to Hollander's arguments is a property [23, Section 4] linking positional
numeration systems to the representation of real numbers via a real base [32, 30, 34, 6, 16].
Whenever the dominant root condition is dropped, this link disappears and hence new tools
are needed in order to attack the general problem.

   The aim of this paper is to provide a complete characterization of positional numera-
tion systems that yield a regular numeration language. We solve this problem in its full
generality, not adding any particular condition on the given positional numeration system.
Our study will lead us to deal with systems that are not associated with a real base as was
the case in Hollander's work. However, we will see that systems with a regular numeration
language are always associated with a very specific way to represent real numbers, namely
by using an alternate base of real numbers as introduced in [12]. This observation was in
fact the original motivation for the study of these new representations of real numbers. In
particular, the notion of Parry alternate base developed in [14] will be central in the present
work since we will see that this condition is necessary in order to ensure the regularity of
the numeration language of a positional numeration system.

   Our main result will be separated into four parts, each handling a different behavior of the
greedy algorithm for the representation of 1 via alternate real bases. Together, these results
yield a semi-decision procedure for deciding the regularity of the numeration language of
a positional numeration system. Testing the ultimate periodicity of the greedy expansions
of 1 in an alternate base (in fact, even in a single real base) is a difficult task, that is not
known to be decidable in general. But, provided that the associated greedy expansions of 1
are known to be finite or ultimately periodic, which we can indeed check in many situations,
our results actually provide us with a genuine decision procedure.

   The article will be structured as follows. In Section 2, we recall the basics of positional
numeration systems and introduce our notation. In Section 3 we show that we can restrict
our study to the case where the base sequence is a linear recurrence sequence. In Section 4,
we explain how to restrict our study to the thin sub-language of the lexicographically
maximal words of each length. We explain how alternate bases naturally arise and recall
the related notions in Section 5, then show how they induce four different types of behavior
within the numeration language in Section 6. We prove the link between lexicographically
maximal words of each length and the associated alternate base in Section 7, allowing a
further restriction to Parry alternate bases only. With the preparatory work done, Section 8
details our strategy for proving the announced criteria. Sections 9, 10, 11 and 12 contain
the bulk of the work, carefully analyzing each of the four cases outlined above and obtaining
a criterion for each of them. In these four sections, we take care of positioning our results
in comparison to those obtained by Hollander, when we restrict our hypotheses to the case
of a dominant root: either we recover the previously known results, or we handle a new
situation, not occurring in the case of a dominant root. In particular, our results allow
4                               ÉMILIE CHARLIER, SAVINIEN KRECZMAN

the possibility of a base to be equal to 1. In the dominant root case, this corresponds to
the polynomial case, which was not treated in [23]. Section 13 summarizes our results and
comments on their effectiveness. We provide two carefully designed examples in order to
illustrate different scenarios. Finally, Sections 14 and 15 answer Hollander's conjecture in
the negative and explain why similar conjectures are unlikely to be true in the non-dominant
root case, concluding the paper.

                             2. Positional numeration systems

   A positional numeration system is given by an increasing sequence U = (Un)n0 of

integers  such  that  U0  =  1  and  the  quotients       Un+1    are  uniformly  bounded.   The  value  of  a
                                                           Un

                                                                    -1

                                valU (w-1 · · · w0) = wnUn.

                                                                    n=0

For a given x  N, any word w with letters in N such that valU (w) = x is said to be a

U -representation of x. Such a representation need not be unique.

   Among all possible U -representations of x, we will consider the one obtained using the

greedy algorithm. First, we let  be the least integer such that x < U and we let r = x.
                                                            rn+1
Then  for  every  n  =   - 1, . . . , 0,  we  set  an  =     Un     and  rn  = rn+1 - anUn.  The  produced

                                            repU (x) := a-1 · · · a0,

which is called the greedy U -representation of x.
   The language of all greedy U -representations, possibly preceded by zeros, i.e., the lan-

guage
                                               LU := 0repU (N),

is called the numeration language. It is written over the alphabet

                                AU := {0, . . . , sup        Un+1      - 1},
                                                              Un

called the numeration alphabet.

   Our aim is to characterize the positional numeration systems giving rise to a regular

numeration language. Note that the languages LU and repU (N) are simultaneously regular.
However, allowing leading zeros will often be more convenient for our future developments.
In particular, a word w-1 · · · w0  AU belongs to LU if and only if

for all n  {0, . . . , }. This also implies that the language LU is suffix-closed.

           3. First step: Restriction to linear numeration systems

   The following well-known result ­ see for instance [35, 27] ­ asserts that we can restrict
our study to linear numeration systems, which are positional numeration systems with the
additional condition that the base sequence U = (Un)n0 is linear over Z: there exists
integers c0, . . . , cm-1 such that

                                Un+m = cm-1Un+m-1 + . . . + c0Un                                         (3.1)
NUMERATION SYSTEMS WITHOUT A DOMINANT ROOT AND REGULARITY                        5

for all n  0. The polynomial
                                 Xm - cm-1Xm-1 - c2Xm-2 - · · · - c0

is called the characteristic polynomial of the linear recurrence relation (3.1).

Proposition 1. Any positional numeration system with a regular numeration language is
linear.

   Let us recall some background on linear sequences that will be useful in our future
analysis. Given a sequence of rational numbers U = (Un)n0, the set of polynomials
{cmXm + cm-1Xm-1 + · · · + c0  Q[X] : n  0, cmUn+m + cm-1Un+m-1 + · · · + c0Un = 0}

is an ideal IU of the ring of polynomials Q[X]. The monic generator of this ideal is called
the minimal polynomial of U . Its roots are called the eigenvalues of U . The multiplicity of
an eigenvalue of U is its multiplicity as a root of the minimal polynomial of U . Now, if U
is an integer sequence that is linear over Z, i.e., if the ideal IU contains a monic polynomial
with integer coefficients, then the minimal polynomial of U also has integer coefficients. We
refer to [5] for more details on linear recurrence sequences.

4. Second step: Restriction to lexicographically maximal words of each
                                                      length

   In this section, we show that we can focus on the regularity of the language of maximal
words of the numeration language. The language of maximal words of a language L over a
totally ordered alphabet is the language

Max(L) := {u  L : for all v  L, |v| = |u| = v lex u},

where lex is the lexicographic order. That is, Max(L) is the language obtained by extract-
ing the lexicographically greatest word of each length present in L. In our case, we may
present an alternative characterization of this language.

   First, let us recall the following well-known property of greedy U -representations; see for
example [28, Chapter 7]. It uses the so-called radix order rad where words are ordered
length by length first, and then lexicographically: u <rad v if either |u| < |v|, or |u| = |v|
and u <lex v.

Lemma 2. Let U be a positional numeration system, let x  N and let w  AU \ 0AU . If
repU (x) <rad w then x < valU (w).

This allows us to obtain the following description of the maximal words in LU .

Lemma 3. Let U be a positional numeration system. Then

Max(LU ) = {repU (Un - 1) : n  N}.

Proof. Clearly, the word repU (Un - 1) belongs to LU for all n. From the greedy algorithm,

we know that |repU (Un - 1)| = n and that every word w in LU of length n is such that

valU (w) < Un. If w starts with 0, then w <lex repU (Un - 1). Otherwise, we get w lex

repU (Un - 1) by Theorem 2.                                                      

   The language Max(LU ) is of great interest to us because it encompasses the regularity
of the whole numeration language LU as shown by the following proposition.
6               ÉMILIE CHARLIER, SAVINIEN KRECZMAN

Proposition 4.

   · If L is a regular language, then the language Max(L) is regular.

   · If U is a positional numeration system such that Max(LU ) is regular, then the
     numeration language LU is also regular.

   For the sake of completeness, we reproduce Shallit's proof of the first item from [35],
and give a new construction of an automaton accepting a numeration language built from
the knowledge of the lexicographically maximal words (provided that they form a regular
language). Another construction of such an automaton was proposed in [23], but the
resulting automaton contains far more states as the one we describe here, since it is obtained
as a product of several automata.

   Also, note that for an arbitrary language L, it is not the case that the regularity of the
language Max(L) implies that of L. For example, the Dyck language of well-parenthesized
binary words is well known to be non-regular whereas its language of maximal words with
the order 0 < 1 is (01), hence is regular. Hence, the hypothesis that the language is derived
from a numeration system is important, as such languages have some structure with respect
to the lexicographic order.

   We first recall two useful lemmas. The first one, already in [23], gives a characterization
of the words in LU in terms of a lexicographic condition of their suffixes.

Lemma 5. Let U be a positional numeration system. A word w-1 · · · w0  AU belongs to
LU if and only if

                                       wn-1 · · · w0 lex repU (Un - 1)

for all n  {0, . . . , }.

Proof. The necessary condition follows from the fact that LU is suffix-closed and Theorem 3.

The sufficient condition is obtained by using (2.1) and an induction on the length of the

words.                                                                 

   The second lemma, proved in [35], provides a useful decomposition of slender regular
languages, i.e., containing a bounded number of words of each length.

Lemma 6. A language is slender and regular if and only if it is a finite union of languages
of the form xyz.

Proof of Theorem 4. We reproduce Shallit's simple argument from [35] for proving the
regularity of the language of lexicographically maximal words of each length of a reg-
ular language. Let L be an arbitrary regular language written over a totally ordered
alphabet (A, <). In order to show that Max(L) is also regular, we can equivalently
show that L \ Max(L) is regular. Let A = (Q, i, F, A, ) be a deterministic finite au-
tomaton accepting L. Consider now the following non-deterministic finite automaton:
B = (Q × Q × {e, }, (i, i, e), F × F × {}, A, R), where the transition relation R contains
the following transitions:

       · (p, q, e) -a ((p, a), (q, a), e) for all p, q  Q and a  A;
       · (p, q, e) -a ((p, a), (q, b), ) for all p, q  Q and a, b  A with a < b;
       · (p, q, ) -a ((p, a), (q, b), ) for all p, q  Q and a, b  A.
NUMERATION SYSTEMS WITHOUT A DOMINANT ROOT AND REGULARITY  7

Transitions in the second component of Q nondeterministically guess a word of L that is
greater than the word read by B. As a result, a given word is accepted by B if and only if
it belongs to L and there exists a lexicographically greater word in L of the same length:
B accepts exactly the words in L \ Max(L).

   Let us now turn to the second item. The proof is constructive, and will be illustrated
in Theorem 8 below. Let U be a positional numeration system and suppose that the

   Studying the regularity of the language Max(LU ) is easier than that of LU itself since
Max(LU ) is a thin language, that is, it contains at most one word of each length [31]. This
allows us to use Theorem 6.

   We introduce one last straightforward lemma, which will allow us to separate the study
of the regularity of Max(LU ) according to the residue class modulo p for some suitable p.

Lemma 9. Let L be a language over a finite alphabet A and let p, N  N with p  1. The
language L is regular if and only if the p languages

                                  {w  L : |w|  i (mod p), |w|  N }

are all regular.

    5. Third step: Emergence of alternate bases associated with regular
                                              numeration systems

   Alternate bases are particular Cantor real bases that were independently introduced
in [10, 12]. As it turns out, the first appearance of these alternating systems of real bases
which gave rise to the study [12] is due to the observations reported in this section. See
[11] for a survey on alternate bases.

   In view of Theorem 10, with a positional numeration system with a regular language can
be associated a p-tuple of real numbers greater than or equal to 1, which correspond to the
p values of the limits. We will see that these p values play a crucial role in our study. This
will be done through the introduction of a new way of representing real numbers by using
these p values in an alternating manner. Note that non-minimal choices of p only lead us to
consider multiples of the minimal possible one, which amounts to repeating the associated
tuple of real numbers. Even though this is not forbidden as it won't be a problem of any
kind for our future developments, it does not bring any interesting feature either. So, in
what follows, we will always assume that p is minimal.

Definition 13. An alternate real base is given by a tuple B = (0, . . . , p-1) of real numbers
greater than or equal to 1. In this system, the B-value of an infinite word a = a0a1 · · ·  NN
is the real number

                                        valB (a)  :=  +         an  ·  n
                                                      n=0  01 · ·

provided that the series converges, where we set n := n mod p for every n, extending B to
a periodic sequence (n)n0.

   Every such sequence a with valB(a) = x is said to be a B-representation of the real
number x. Unless we are in the degenerate case where p = 1 and 0 = 1, we can use a
greedy algorithm to find a specific B-representation of a real number x  [0, 1], which will

be called the B-expansion of x. We set r0 := x. Then, for n  N, we compute an := nrn
and rn+1 := nrn - nrn. The sequence a0a1a2 · · · of greedy digits is denoted by dB(1).
It is easily checked that this is indeed a B-representation of x. Whenever B = (0) = (1),
the greedy algorithm works only for x  {0, 1}, in which case we set dB(1) := 10.

   Among these expansions, we will be mostly interested in the expansion of 1, not only
in the base B but also in all the bases obtained as circular permutations of B. For B =
(0, . . . , p-1) and i  {0, . . . , p - 1}, we let

                                        di := dB(i) (1)
       NUMERATION SYSTEMS WITHOUT A DOMINANT ROOT AND REGULARITY                                 13

where B(i) := (i, . . . , i+p-1) denotes the i-th circular shift of the base B. Again, it will
be convenient to extend this notation to dn for all n, where the index n is seen modulo p.
In particular, we have dnp = d0 for all n.

   We say that a representation is finite if it ends in a tail of zeros, and infinite otherwise.
In our study, the case where a B(i)-expansion of 1 is finite will require additional care, as

will be apparent over time. We describe how to obtain from such a representation a new
infinite one which is maximal among all infinite B(i)-representations of 1. The obtained
infinite sequence is called the quasi-greedy B(i)-expansion of 1, is denoted by di, and is
computed thanks to a recursive process as follows:

di :=  di,                                      if di is infinite ;
       ti,0ti,1 · · · ti,i-2(ti,i-1 - 1)di+i ,  if di = ti,0ti,1 · · · ti,i-10 with ti,i-1 > 0.

erate case where B = 0 = 1, we obtain d0 = 0, which is clearly not a B-representation
of 1. Note that, in this degenerate case, no infinite representation of 1 exists.

Remark 30. As in Theorem 26, we argue that the condition (c) of Theorem 29 can be used
effectively to decide the regularity of a given Li, assuming the eigenvalues of U are known.
Since the sequence i satisfies the same recurrence relations as U , its eigenvalues form a
subset of those of U and can be computed effectively. It then suffices to check whether
these eigenvalues are all zero or roots of unity, which is equivalent to i being ultimately
periodic.

not be regular. Let us illustrate this comment with two examples.

   In this section, we examine the regularity of Li when i is part of a cycle in the graph
G. In this case, there exists some r such that r(i) = i. Consequently, di, . . . , dr-1(i)
are all finite and di = (di · · · d r-1(i)). We know that, up to taking large enough n, the
words repU (Unp-i - 1) share prefixes of arbitrary length with one of the wi,j's. However,
these choices for all vertices of the cycle are not independent of one another, which brings

additional information on top of Theorem 18. This observation will be made clear shortly

as it will be one of the main arguments in what follows.

cycle" that will allow us to focus on ultimately periodic sequences.

Remark 38. As in the previous sections, Theorem 37 can be used effectively in order to

decide the regularity of all the languages Li from a cycle. If the eigenvalues of U are known,
then those of the sequences j(i) can be computed, allowing us to test whether they are
all ultimately periodic. If this is indeed the case, then the values of M, M  and i(,Me r) can
be computed, and the condition (d) of Theorem 37 can be tested.

   In comparison with [23], this result is new. It provides a necessary and sufficient condition

for the regularity of LU in the simple Parry dominant root case, which is precisely the
case that Hollander did not solve entirely. In particular, Hollander exhibited an example

showing that the regularity of LU can depend on the initial conditions, and not only on the
characteristic polynomial of a linear recurrence satisfied by U . The example is the following.

Suppose that U satisfies the linear recurrence of characteristic polynomial (X - 1)(X - 3).

This exactly means that the sequence  is constant as this sequence is given by n =
Un - 3Un-1, thus it satisfies the linear recurrence of characteristic polynomial X - 1. As
shown by Hollander, by choosing the initial conditions U0 = 1, U1 = 4, we obtain a regular
numeration language, whereas by choosing the initial conditions U0 = 1, U1 = 2, we obtain
a non-regular numeration language. This situation was not handled by Hollander's result

but is covered by Theorem 39. The notation drastically reduces since the dominant root
of the system is 3 and  is constant, hence we get  = N = M = M  = 1. For the initial

conditions U0 = 1, U1 = 4, we get that Un = 3Un-1 +1 and n = 1 for all n  1. Therefore,
Theorem 39 tells us that LU is regular. However, for the initial conditions U0 = 1, U1 = 2,
    NUMERATION SYSTEMS WITHOUT A DOMINANT ROOT AND REGULARITY                         37

we  get that  Un  =  3n+1  and  n  = -1  for  all  n  1.  In  this  case, Theorem 39  yields that

LU is not regular.

The results of this section also include the case where U has 1 as a dominant root. We

note that this case was not considered at all in [23]. We discuss this particular case in the

next corollary.

Corollary 40. Let U be a positional numeration system with the dominant root 1. Then the
numeration language LU is regular if and only if the sequence (Un+1 - Un)n0 is ultimately
periodic.

   In particular, if the sequence U is ultimately a polynomial, i.e., there exists a polynomial
P  C[X] and an integer N  0 such that Un = P (n) for all n  N , then the numeration
language LU is regular if and only if this polynomial has integer coefficients and degree 1,
i.e., there exists a, b  Z with a > 0 such that Un = an + b for all n  N .

Proof. As for Theorem 39, under the dominant root hypothesis, the notation of this section

reduces to p = 1, i = 0, r = 1, ki,r = . Moreover, since the dominant root is 1, we also
have  = 1 and the sequence  is given by n = Un - Un-1 for n  1. By Theorem 39,
if LU is regular then  is ultimately periodic. Let us argue that the converse also holds.
Suppose that  is ultimately periodic with preperiod N  1 and period M  1. With the
notation of Theorem 39, we have M  = M and in order to obtain that LU is regular, it
suffices to show that

                           M -1          M -1

                                 N+j = (UN+j - UN+j-1)  0.

                           j=0           j=0

This is clearly the case as U is an increasing sequence of integers.

The particular case is straightforward.                                               

Example 41. The sequence U given by the initial conditions U0 = 1, U1 = 2 and the

relation Un = Un-2 + 3 for n  2 yields a regular numeration language as (Un+1 - Un)n1 =
(1, 2, 1, 2, . . .). Indeed, it easily checked that LU = 10  1(00)1  {}. On the other hand,
Shallit proved in [35] that the numeration system U given by Un = (n+1)2 for all n  0 has

a non-regular numeration language. This result can be recovered by the characterization

given in Theorem 40.

   Finally, similarly to the discussion ending Section 9, let us explain how the second part
of Hollander's main result from [23] can be re-obtained as a consequence of Theorem 39.

                                  12. Vertices leading to a cycle

   This is the final case in our discussion. We are now focusing on vertices i in the graph
G that have a non-trivial path leading to a cycle in G. In this case, there exists s  1
and r  1 such that s+r(i) = s(i). The expansions di, . . . , ds+r-1(i) are all finite and
di = di · · · d s-1(i)(d s(i) · · · ds+r-1(i)). In the remainder of this section, we assume that
s  1 is minimal such that there exists r  1 with s+r(i) = s(i), to avoid duplicating the
previous case. As for Section 10, we note that this situation does not occur in the dominant
root case of [23], i.e., whenever p = 1. We begin with a lemma.

Lemma 43. For any sequence (xn)n0 of complex numbers and any positive integer M ,
the following conditions are equivalent.

    (a) The sequence (xn)n0 is a linear recurrence sequence and all its nonzero eigenvalues
          are M -th roots of unity and have multiplicity at most 2.

    (b) The sequence (xn+M - xn)n0 is ultimately periodic with period M .

1, . . . , d be the nonzero eigenvalues of (xn)n0. Then there exist N  0 and a1, . . . , ad,

   Now that we have reduced our study to linear sequences with eigenvalues that are roots
of unity with multiplicity at most 2, we investigate precisely which of these sequences lead
to regular languages. This is the point of our next and final main result. We will see that
although eigenvalues of multiplicity 2 may occur, these occurrences are heavily constrained.
In fact, only one new type of behavior arises.

Remark 48. Let us argue that the condition (c) of Theorem 47 can be used effectively.

Once the eigenvalues of U are known, we can find the eigenvalues of the sequences j(i),
for j  {0, . . . , s - 1}, and check whether these sequences all satisfy the condition (a) of

Theorem 43. If this is the case, and assuming that we already know that the sequences

Theorem 47) can be computed. From there, the values i,e,j and (Ms(ir),)e can be computed,
and Theorem 47 can be used to decide the regularity of Li.

                                         13. Decision procedure

   The results of this work can be used in practice to decide if the language LU associated
with any given positional numeration system U is regular. In this section, we describe the
semi-decision procedure induced by our results, namely Theorems 21, 25, 29, 32, 37, 44
and 47. Below, we will argue that in the situation where the obtained alternate base is
Parry, we indeed get a decision procedure.

    (1) Using Theorem 1, identify the values of p and 0, . . . , p-1.
    (2) Compute the infinite words d0, . . . , dp-1 and the graph G. By Theorem 21, if one

          of the infinite words d0, . . . , dp-1 is aperiodic, then LU is not regular. In this case,
          the algorithm stops with "no".
    (3) Otherwise, study the regularity of the languages L0, . . . , Lp-1.
           (a) For each vertex i with no outgoing edge, use the item (c) of Theorem 25 to

                check whether the corresponding languages Li is regular or not. As soon as
                one can find a non-regular such language, the algorithm stops with "no".
          (b) Proceed with the vertices i leading to a vertex with no outgoing edge, starting
                with the vertices at distance 1, then distance 2, etc. For each such vertex i, use
                the item (c) of Theorem 29 to decide whether the corresponding language Li
                is regular. As soon as one can find a non-regular such language, the algorithm
                stops with "no".
           (c) For each cycle in G, first check whether every sequence i with i in the cycle
                is ultimately periodic. If at least one of them is not, then the algorithm stops
                with "no", following Theorem 32. Otherwise, find a common period M of these
                sequences such that M p is a multiple of ki,r where r is the length of the cycle
                and i is any vertex of the cycle. Then use the item (d) of Theorem 37 to decide
                whether all languages Li, with i in the cycle, are regular. If at least one of
                them is not regular, the algorithm stops with "no".
          (d) Finally, consider the vertices i leading to a cycle, starting with the vertices at
                distance 1, then distance 2, etc. For each such vertex i, use Theorem 44 and
                the item (c) of Theorem 47 to decide whether the corresponding language Li
NUMERATION SYSTEMS WITHOUT A DOMINANT ROOT AND REGULARITY                                45

                is regular. As soon as one can find a non-regular such language, the algorithm
                stops with "no".
    (4) If the languages Li for all i in the graph have been checked to be regular, then LU
          itself is regular. The algorithm stops with "yes".

   Note that, at step (3), we can run the tests in parallel, for each path to either a vertex
with no outgoing edge or a cycle. First, we can consider all the vertices with no outgoing
edge and the cycles, and then proceed iteratively with the vertices at distance d  1 to
such vertices or cycles, for increasing values of d until we have considered all vertices of the
graph.

   The greedy algorithm provides a semi-algorithm for testing if a given expansion of 1 is
ultimately periodic: we may simply generate digits ti and memorize the remainders ri that
appear in the algorithm (to recall, ti = iri and ri+1 = iri - ti). If two remainders
are equal, then the algorithm loops and the expansion of 1 is ultimately periodic. In
particular, we have a semi-algorithm that tests whether a given alternate base is Parry.
However, testing when an alternate base is not Parry is harder. Techniques such as those
of Section 15 can sometimes be applied, but there is no known general algorithm.

   If we assume that the eigenvalues of U are known and that the associated alternate base
is known to be Parry, Theorems 26, 30, 38 and 48 ensure that the above procedure can be
carried out effectively.

   We now illustrate the above decision procedure with two examples, chosen to present a
variety of behaviors.

Example 50. Let us consider the system U generated by the recurrence relation

                 Un+18 = 23Un+15 + 5Un+12 - 46Un+9 - 7Un+6 + 23Un+3 + 3Un
and the initial conditions

                    14. Comments on Hollander's original conjecture

   In this section, we go back to Hollander's original conjecture, which was the starting
point for this research. We restate it with our notation.

Conjecture 52 ([23], Section 8.2). If L is regular, there exists p such that the limit
                                                  lim Unp+i
                                                 n U(n-1)p+i

exists and is independent of i. Furthermore, the minimal polynomial P of the recurrence
relation satisfied by U is of the form P (X) = Q(Xp) where Q is the minimal polynomial
for a recurrence which gives rise to a regular language.
48          ÉMILIE CHARLIER, SAVINIEN KRECZMAN

   We should note that in [23] this conjecture is given in the form of a comment rather
than a formal statement. Therefore, some parts of the statement are difficult to interpret
unambiguously. In particular, it is not clear in Hollander's statement whether P must be
the minimal polynomial of U , rather than any polynomial associated with a recurrence
relation satisfied by U .

   The first part of the statement was proven in Theorem 10. For the second part of the
statement, we give two examples that refute the conjecture as written above and provide a
reason to disbelieve the interpretation where P need not be minimal.

Example 53. Consider again item (5) of Theorem 19, i.e., the system U generated by the

recurrence relation Un+3 = 2Un+2 - 4Un+1 + 8Un and the initial conditions (U0, U1, U2) =

(1, 3, 8).  It can be seen that LU  is regular in this case,  and  that  limn   Un   =  16.
                                                                               Un-4

Nevertheless, the minimal polynomial of U is X3 - 2X2 + 4X - 8, which is not of the form

Q(X 4 ).

   The next example illustrates a more fundamental objection to the conjecture. There
exists an alternate base which is Parry but whose product of elements is not Parry (in the
non-alternate sense). For such a base, even if its minimal polynomial is of the form Q(Xp),
the polynomial Q cannot be the minimal polynomial of a sequence giving rise to a regular
language.

Example 54. Consider the system U generated by the recurrence relation Un+6 = 9Un+3 -
9Un and the initial conditions (U0, U1, U2, U3, U4, U5) = (1, 2, 3, 9, 15, 24). In this case, the
numeration language LU is again regular. However, the associated alternate base is (3, , )
where  is the golden ratio, and 32 is not a Parry number. Therefore, X2-9X +9 is not the

minimal polynomial of a recurrence which gives rise to a regular language, independently of

the choice of initial conditions. Note that taking multiples of p cannot fix this as no power
of 32 is a Parry number. Indeed, no power of 32 is a Pisot number and it is known that

Parry and Pisot numbers of degree 2 coincide [1].

   The latter example does not completely refute Hollander's conjecture in the setting where
P is not assumed to be minimal, but for the conjecture to hold there would need to exist
a Parry number such that X2 - 9X + 9 is a factor of its Parry polynomial (and similarly
for any Parry alternate base whose product of elements is not a Parry number).

   15. Why obtaining criteria for regularity relying only on recurrence
                             relations satisfied by U is not achievable

   The results in Hollander [23] are of a different nature compared to ours. Rather than
extracting new sequences from U and deciding the regularity of LU based on them, Hollan-
der aims to link directly the regularity of LU with polynomials giving recurrence relations
satisfied by U , which is a more tractable criterion. The aim of this section is to present
evidence that we cannot replicate this in our setting.

   Indeed, in Hollander's case with p = 1, the knowledge of the minimal polynomial P of
U gives us the value of the dominant root , from where Hollander's study can take place.
In our case however, knowing the minimal polynomial of U only tells us the value of the
product of all bases,  = 0 · · · p-1, but does not inform us on the values of 0, . . . , p-1
themselves. As a result, the behavior of U rarely depends on just the minimal polynomial.
            NUMERATION SYSTEMS WITHOUT A DOMINANT ROOT AND REGULARITY                                                              49

We illustrate this by exhibiting a polynomial P and various sets of initial conditions that
lead to differing behaviors for U .

maximal modulus, which are -  and  where   2.80 is the dominant root of the

polynomial X4 - 2X3 - 2X2 - 2. Consequently, a generic increasing sequence that satisfies

this recurrence relation is associated with an alternate base of length 2.

the numeration language is regular in this case. In fact, the maximal words are exactly the

prefixes of the quasi-greedy expansions d0 = (11010000) and d1 = (10100001), depending
on the parity of their length.

From the recursive definition of di , we will be lead to combine the expansions with respect
to the p circular shifts of the alternate base B in order to be able to compute a quasi-greedy
expansion. In order to emphasize these links between the different shifted bases, we define
a directed graph G in the following way. The set of vertices of G is {0, . . . , p - 1}. There is
an edge going from i to (i + i) mod p if di is finite of length i. This defines a graph where
each vertex has outdegree at most 1. Whenever it exists, we let (i) denote the successor
of i, i.e.,

                                            (i) := (i + i) mod p.

This allows us to separate the vertices of G into four categories:

    (1) Vertices i with no successor.
    (2) Vertices i leading to a vertex with no successor, i.e., such that there exists r  1

          such that r(i) has no successor.
    (3) Vertices i within a cycle, i.e., such that there exists r  1 with r(i) = i.
    (4) Vertices i leading to a cycle, i.e., such that there exists r  1 such that r(i) belongs

          to a cycle.

Each of these categories will be treated separately in the proof of our main result.
   The digits of the greedy expansions will be denoted by ti,n for n  0, i.e.,

                                               di := ti,0ti,1ti,2 · · ·

                                      di = ti,0ti,1 · · · ti,i-2(ti,i-1 - 1)

whenever di = ti,0ti,1 · · · ti,i-10 with ti,i-1 > 1. In this case, we will always keep the
notation i to refer to the length of di, i.e., the length of its prefix up to the last non-zero
digit, which we denote by

                                             di = ti,0ti,1 · · · ti,i-1.

Thus, in this situation, we have
                                                  di = didi+i .

Note that we use bold letters to designate infinite words while we use a normal font for
finite words. In particular, to avoid any confusion, we always write tails of zeros explicitly
in infinite words.

   In order to iterate the quasi-greedy process, we define

     ki,j := i + (i) + 2(i) + . . . + j-1(i)

     · ki,0 = 0 and ki,1 = i

                 7. Fourth step: Restriction to Parry alternate bases

   The next result is one of the key arguments of our proof. It connects the lexicographically
maximal words of each length in the numeration language to the representations of 1 in the
associated alternate base.

   We introduce the following notation, which will allow us to include alternate bases
(0, . . . , p-1) with some i equal to 1. As previously discussed, such alternate bases can
be linked to certain linear numeration systems, and therefore must be taken into account
in our study.
    NUMERATION SYSTEMS WITHOUT A DOMINANT ROOT AND REGULARITY                                              17

Definition 17. Let U be a positional numeration system with an associated alternate base
(0, . . . , p-1). Then for integers i, c, n such that 0  i < p, n  1 and 1  c  Unp-i, we
define

                                       repi,c(n) := 0repU (Unp-i - c),

where  = np - i - |repU (Unp-i - c)|.

   The idea is that we pad the greedy representation of Unp-i - c with leading zeros in order
to obtain a representation of length np - i. Most of the time, this consists in doing nothing
since if i > 1, then repi,c(n) = repU (Unp-i - c) for all large enough n. Moreover, we have
repi,1(n) = repU (Unp-i - 1) for all n  1. However, in the case where i = 1 and c  2,
these few leading zeros will ensure that we keep working with words of the desired length
np - i.

   Let us extract some useful information from Theorem 18 in the case where di is infinite.
In terms of the graph G, this means that i is a vertex with no outgoing edge.

Corollary 20. Let U be a positional numeration system with an associated alternate base

Proof. Since di = di, only j = 0 is possible in Theorem 18.     

   In Section 5, we have seen that any positional numeration system U with a regular

numeration language has an associated alternate real base B = (0, . . . , p-1). The next
result provides the additional information that this associated alternate base B must have
the property that di is ultimately periodic for every i  {0, . . . , p - 1}. Alternate bases
with this property are said to be Parry, see [14]. Equivalently, one can ask that di is finite
or ultimately periodic for every i  {0, . . . , p - 1}, see [12, Proposition 40].

Proposition 21. Let U be a positional numeration system with a regular numeration lan-
guage. Then its associated alternate base is Parry.

Proof. Let p be the length of the alternate base and consider i  {0, . . . , p - 1} such that di

is infinite. We have to show that di is ultimately periodic. By Theorem 20, the sequence of

finite words (repU (Unp-i - 1))n1 converges to the infinite word di. Theorems 4, 6 and 9

then imply that di is ultimately periodic.                      

                                              8. Our strategy

   We consider an arbitrary positional numeration system U and we aim at determining
whether the numeration language LU is regular or not. At this point, we have obtained
several necessary conditions for LU to be regular. We thus put ourselves in the restricted
situation where these conditions are satisfied. Namely, we suppose that U is linear and
that there is a Parry alternate base B = (0, . . . , p-1) associated with U . In view of the
results of Section 4, in order to understand when LU is indeed regular, it suffices to study
the regularity of the p languages

                                      Li := {repU (Unp-i - 1) : n  1}.

Either these p languages are all regular, in which case, the numeration language LU is
regular, or one of them is not regular, in which case LU is not regular.

   We will see that the regularities of these p languages are interconnected. Our approach
is based on the graph G which is meant to encode the connections between the p shifts of
the alternate base when performing the quasi-greedy algorithm. We will consider the four
NUMERATION SYSTEMS WITHOUT A DOMINANT ROOT AND REGULARITY                    21

families of vertices i that we already introduced in Section 6. After dealing with these four
cases separately, we will combine them in order to describe a decision procedure that will
allow us to determine whether or not the numeration language LU is regular. These results
will not be illustrated until Section 13, where two appropriate examples will be presented to
exhibit a variety of behaviors. We invite the reader to consult Theorem 51 and Theorem 50,
for Sections 9 and 10, and Sections 11 and 12, respectively.

   Since the regularities of the languages Li with i  {0, . . . , p - 1} are linked together, we
will be lead to not only consider the maximal words of each length, but also words of the
form repU (Un - c) where c is a constant. Note that Theorem 18 was already stated in this
spirit. The following definition will be used in the statements of the four main theorems
that describe the situation for each category of vertices in the graph G.

Definition 22. For i  {0, . . . , p - 1} and positive integers c, we define

                                   Li,c := {repi,c(n) : n  1, Unp-i  c}

where the notation repi,c(n) has been defined in Theorem 17.

   Again, the condition that Unp-i  c will not be a true restriction as for any N  0, the
language Li,c is regular if and only if so is the language Li,c  {w  AU : |w|  N }. Note
that we always have Li = Li,1 as repi,1(n) = repU (Unp-i - 1) for all n  1.

9. Vertices with no outgoing edge

means that the greedy and the quasi-greedy B(i)-expansions of 1 coincide, i.e., di = di .
Since we are dealing with a Parry alternate base, this infinite word is ultimately periodic.
We let q0 be the minimal preperiod of di and we let m0 be its minimal period that is a

Proposition 26. Assume that the eigenvalues of U are known and let i  {0, . . . , p - 1}

   In the dominant root case studied by Hollander, Theorem 25 corresponds to the case
where  is a non-simple Parry number; see [23, Lemmas 7.3 and 7.4]. In this case, we have
p = 1 and we only have to consider the sequence q,m defined by

ultimately zero if and only if the base sequence U ultimately satisfies the linear recurrence

                                         q+m                                                        q

Such a polynomial Pq,m is called an extended -polynomial by Hollander. In particular,
whenever q and m are chosen to be the minimal preperiod q0 and period m0 of d(1), we
obtain the so-called Parry polynomial Pq0,m0, also called the -polynomial. As noted by
Hollander, all extended -polynomials can be obtained by multiplying the Parry polynomial

Pq0,m0 by some very specific polynomials, as we have

                      Pq,km0 = Xq-q0 (1 + Xm0 + · · · + X(k-1)m0 )Pq0,m0                                                        (9.2)

for any q  q0 and k  1.
   With these comments, we see that the first part of the main result of [23] can be re-

obtained as a corollary of Theorem 25.

Corollary 27 ([23]). Let U be a positional numeration system with a dominant root  > 1

such that d(1) is ultimately periodic, i.e.,  is a non-simple Parry number. The numeration
language LU is regular if and only if the base sequence U satisfies a linear recurrence relation
whose characteristic polynomial is given by an extended -polynomial.
NUMERATION SYSTEMS WITHOUT A DOMINANT ROOT AND REGULARITY  25

   The relationships given in Theorem 24 can be viewed as an analogue of (9.2). However, in
the general setting considered in this paper, i.e., with possibly p  2, there are no such nice
polynomials associated with the sequences i,q,m. This makes the situation more complex
and forces us to work with the graph G as a whole rather than to independently consider
each vertex i of G.

               10. Vertices leading to a vertex with no outgoing edge

   In this section, we investigate the regularity of Li when there is a non-trivial path from
i to a vertex s(i) with no outgoing edge in the graph G. This means that di is finite but,
after s  1 steps, the quasi-greedy algorithm sees an infinite expansion ds(i) and stops.
Note that this situation never occurs whenever p = 1, that is, whenever the numeration
system U has a dominant root. As in the previous section, our proofs will rely on the
introduction of an auxiliary sequence . However, the definition of  must be adapted to
account for the finiteness of our expansions. This definition will be used in this section as
well as the two following ones.

Definition 28. For i  {0, . . . , p - 1} such that di is finite and for all integers n such that
np - i  i, we let

                                                                                   i

                                    (i)n = Unp-i - ti,-1Unp-i-.

                                                                                 =1

   As before, we are only concerned with such values for large n, so we usually omit to
verify the condition np - i  i. We will be interested not only in the values of i for the
current i, but also for its successors h(i) in the graph G, for h  {0, . . . , s - 1}.

                                                                           ÉMILIE CHARLIER, SAVINIEN KRECZMAN

                                               Abstract. Positional numeration systems are a large family of numeration systems used
                                               to represent natural numbers. Whether the set of all representations forms a regular
                                               language or not is one of the most important questions that can be asked of such a system.
                                               This question was investigated in a 1998 article by Hollander. Central to his analysis is
                                               a property linking positional numeration systems and Rényi numeration systems, which
                                               use a real base to represent real numbers. However, this link only exists when the initial
                                               numeration system has a dominant root, which is not a necessary condition for regularity.
                                               In this article, we show a more general link between positional numeration systems and
                                               alternate base numeration systems, a family generalizing Rényi systems. We then take
                                               advantage of this link to provide a full characterization of those numeration systems
                                               that generate a regular language. We also discuss the effectiveness of our method, and
                                               comment Hollander's results and conjecture in the light of ours.

                                               1. Introduction

   If we are to compute operations on numbers (which could be integers, real numbers,
Gaussian integers, complex numbers, or even p-adic numbers), we first need to agree on a
way to represent these numbers. The theory of numeration systems examines the different
methods that can be used to represent numbers through sequences of symbols. Depending
on the tasks we are interested in performing, we can then try to select the most suitable
numeration system. A desirable property of the chosen system is that the operations of
interest can be performed by some finite state machine.

   In this paper, we consider the representation of non-negative integers via positional nu-
meration systems as initiated by Fraenkel [19]. As explained in the nice chapter by Frougny
and Sakarovitch [21], perhaps the most fundamental question to be asked is to understand
which positional numeration systems support a regular set of representations. That is, do
all valid expansions form a regular language in the sense of finite automata? Indeed, the
regularity of the set of expansions is a necessary condition to the use of automata-theoretic
techniques in relation to numeration systems. We can mention the ability to normalize
representations with transducers [20, 22], which enables the computation of addition in the
numeration system using finite state machines. In turn, this allows us to use tools such as
Walnut[29, 36] to automatically prove results related to the numeration system, following
a connection to first-order logic pioneered by Büchi [9].

   Most of the commonly used numeration systems, even in the non-standard numeration
systems community, have the property to generate a regular numeration language. This is
the case of all Bertrand numeration systems associated with a Parry number. These define
a very constrained family of positional numeration systems since there are only one or two
Bertrand numeration systems associated with a given Parry number [7, 15]. All integer
base systems as well as the Zeckendorf numeration system [37] based on the Fibonacci
sequence are Bertrand numeration systems. Another family with this property is that
of Pisot numeration systems, which are the positional numeration systems defined by a
linear recurrence relation whose characteristic polynomial is the minimal polynomial of a
Pisot number [22, 8]. This time, many Pisot numeration systems are associated with one
given Pisot number, since the initial conditions can be more freely chosen. Nevertheless,
this family is still very special, in particular because of the irreducibility constraint on the
characteristic polynomial. These two families share the property of having a dominant root,
meaning that the quotient of consecutive terms in the base sequence admits a limit, which
in addition is greater than one. On the other hand, even some simple numeration systems,
like the one based on the sequence of squares, do not support a regular set of representations
[35].

   As an attempt to unify the theory of numeration systems with a regular numeration
language, Lecomte and Rigo defined the family of abstract numeration systems [25, 26].
Here, the point of view is reversed. One starts with any given regular language, orders the
words in the language with respect to the radix order (i.e., by length first and then using
the lexicographic order within each length) and declares that a non-negative integer n is
represented by the n-th word in the language. This framework encompasses the previously
mentioned families of numeration systems as well as others, such as the Dumont-Thomas
numeration systems built from a substitution [17]. The price of this very general point of
view is that we lose the information of the algorithm to directly produce the representation
NUMERATION SYSTEMS WITHOUT A DOMINANT ROOT AND REGULARITY  3

of a number. This raises the question of determining which regular languages can be
produced by a positional numeration system. This problem was studied in [24] for the
family of Dumont-Thomas numeration systems.

   The question of characterizing positional systems generating a regular numeration lan-
guage was addressed by Hollander in the case where the numeration system satisfies the
dominant root condition [23]. In his study, Hollander provided a detailed, however not full,
description of systems with a dominant root and giving rise to a regular set of representa-
tions. In particular, he does not entirely solves the issue of the dependence to the initial
conditions. Central to Hollander's arguments is a property [23, Section 4] linking positional
numeration systems to the representation of real numbers via a real base [32, 30, 34, 6, 16].
Whenever the dominant root condition is dropped, this link disappears and hence new tools
are needed in order to attack the general problem.

   The aim of this paper is to provide a complete characterization of positional numera-
tion systems that yield a regular numeration language. We solve this problem in its full
generality, not adding any particular condition on the given positional numeration system.
Our study will lead us to deal with systems that are not associated with a real base as was
the case in Hollander's work. However, we will see that systems with a regular numeration
language are always associated with a very specific way to represent real numbers, namely
by using an alternate base of real numbers as introduced in [12]. This observation was in
fact the original motivation for the study of these new representations of real numbers. In
particular, the notion of Parry alternate base developed in [14] will be central in the present
work since we will see that this condition is necessary in order to ensure the regularity of
the numeration language of a positional numeration system.

   Our main result will be separated into four parts, each handling a different behavior of the
greedy algorithm for the representation of 1 via alternate real bases. Together, these results
yield a semi-decision procedure for deciding the regularity of the numeration language of
a positional numeration system. Testing the ultimate periodicity of the greedy expansions
of 1 in an alternate base (in fact, even in a single real base) is a difficult task, that is not
known to be decidable in general. But, provided that the associated greedy expansions of 1
are known to be finite or ultimately periodic, which we can indeed check in many situations,
our results actually provide us with a genuine decision procedure.

   The article will be structured as follows. In Section 2, we recall the basics of positional
numeration systems and introduce our notation. In Section 3 we show that we can restrict
our study to the case where the base sequence is a linear recurrence sequence. In Section 4,
we explain how to restrict our study to the thin sub-language of the lexicographically
maximal words of each length. We explain how alternate bases naturally arise and recall
the related notions in Section 5, then show how they induce four different types of behavior
within the numeration language in Section 6. We prove the link between lexicographically
maximal words of each length and the associated alternate base in Section 7, allowing a
further restriction to Parry alternate bases only. With the preparatory work done, Section 8
details our strategy for proving the announced criteria. Sections 9, 10, 11 and 12 contain
the bulk of the work, carefully analyzing each of the four cases outlined above and obtaining
a criterion for each of them. In these four sections, we take care of positioning our results
in comparison to those obtained by Hollander, when we restrict our hypotheses to the case
of a dominant root: either we recover the previously known results, or we handle a new
situation, not occurring in the case of a dominant root. In particular, our results allow
4                               ÉMILIE CHARLIER, SAVINIEN KRECZMAN

the possibility of a base to be equal to 1. In the dominant root case, this corresponds to
the polynomial case, which was not treated in [23]. Section 13 summarizes our results and
comments on their effectiveness. We provide two carefully designed examples in order to
illustrate different scenarios. Finally, Sections 14 and 15 answer Hollander's conjecture in
the negative and explain why similar conjectures are unlikely to be true in the non-dominant
root case, concluding the paper.

   A positional numeration system is given by an increasing sequence U = (Un)n0 of

           3. First step: Restriction to linear numeration systems

   The following well-known result ­ see for instance [35, 27] ­ asserts that we can restrict
our study to linear numeration systems, which are positional numeration systems with the
additional condition that the base sequence U = (Un)n0 is linear over Z: there exists
integers c0, . . . , cm-1 such that

                                Un+m = cm-1Un+m-1 + . . . + c0Un                                         (3.1)
NUMERATION SYSTEMS WITHOUT A DOMINANT ROOT AND REGULARITY                        5

for all n  0. The polynomial
                                 Xm - cm-1Xm-1 - c2Xm-2 - · · · - c0

is called the characteristic polynomial of the linear recurrence relation (3.1).

Proposition 1. Any positional numeration system with a regular numeration language is
linear.

   Let us recall some background on linear sequences that will be useful in our future
analysis. Given a sequence of rational numbers U = (Un)n0, the set of polynomials
{cmXm + cm-1Xm-1 + · · · + c0  Q[X] : n  0, cmUn+m + cm-1Un+m-1 + · · · + c0Un = 0}

is an ideal IU of the ring of polynomials Q[X]. The monic generator of this ideal is called
the minimal polynomial of U . Its roots are called the eigenvalues of U . The multiplicity of
an eigenvalue of U is its multiplicity as a root of the minimal polynomial of U . Now, if U
is an integer sequence that is linear over Z, i.e., if the ideal IU contains a monic polynomial
with integer coefficients, then the minimal polynomial of U also has integer coefficients. We
refer to [5] for more details on linear recurrence sequences.

4. Second step: Restriction to lexicographically maximal words of each
                                                      length

   In this section, we show that we can focus on the regularity of the language of maximal
words of the numeration language. The language of maximal words of a language L over a
totally ordered alphabet is the language

Max(L) := {u  L : for all v  L, |v| = |u| = v lex u},

where lex is the lexicographic order. That is, Max(L) is the language obtained by extract-
ing the lexicographically greatest word of each length present in L. In our case, we may
present an alternative characterization of this language.

   First, let us recall the following well-known property of greedy U -representations; see for
example [28, Chapter 7]. It uses the so-called radix order rad where words are ordered
length by length first, and then lexicographically: u <rad v if either |u| < |v|, or |u| = |v|
and u <lex v.

Lemma 2. Let U be a positional numeration system, let x  N and let w  AU \ 0AU . If
repU (x) <rad w then x < valU (w).

This allows us to obtain the following description of the maximal words in LU .

Lemma 3. Let U be a positional numeration system. Then

Max(LU ) = {repU (Un - 1) : n  N}.

Proof. Clearly, the word repU (Un - 1) belongs to LU for all n. From the greedy algorithm,

we know that |repU (Un - 1)| = n and that every word w in LU of length n is such that

valU (w) < Un. If w starts with 0, then w <lex repU (Un - 1). Otherwise, we get w lex

repU (Un - 1) by Theorem 2.                                                      

   The language Max(LU ) is of great interest to us because it encompasses the regularity
of the whole numeration language LU as shown by the following proposition.
6               ÉMILIE CHARLIER, SAVINIEN KRECZMAN

Proposition 4.

   · If L is a regular language, then the language Max(L) is regular.

   · If U is a positional numeration system such that Max(LU ) is regular, then the
     numeration language LU is also regular.

   For the sake of completeness, we reproduce Shallit's proof of the first item from [35],
and give a new construction of an automaton accepting a numeration language built from
the knowledge of the lexicographically maximal words (provided that they form a regular
language). Another construction of such an automaton was proposed in [23], but the
resulting automaton contains far more states as the one we describe here, since it is obtained
as a product of several automata.

   Also, note that for an arbitrary language L, it is not the case that the regularity of the
language Max(L) implies that of L. For example, the Dyck language of well-parenthesized
binary words is well known to be non-regular whereas its language of maximal words with
the order 0 < 1 is (01), hence is regular. Hence, the hypothesis that the language is derived
from a numeration system is important, as such languages have some structure with respect
to the lexicographic order.

   We first recall two useful lemmas. The first one, already in [23], gives a characterization
of the words in LU in terms of a lexicographic condition of their suffixes.

Lemma 5. Let U be a positional numeration system. A word w-1 · · · w0  AU belongs to
LU if and only if

                                       wn-1 · · · w0 lex repU (Un - 1)

for all n  {0, . . . , }.

Proof. The necessary condition follows from the fact that LU is suffix-closed and Theorem 3.

The sufficient condition is obtained by using (2.1) and an induction on the length of the

words.                                                                 

   The second lemma, proved in [35], provides a useful decomposition of slender regular
languages, i.e., containing a bounded number of words of each length.

Lemma 6. A language is slender and regular if and only if it is a finite union of languages
of the form xyz.

Proof of Theorem 4. We reproduce Shallit's simple argument from [35] for proving the
regularity of the language of lexicographically maximal words of each length of a reg-
ular language. Let L be an arbitrary regular language written over a totally ordered
alphabet (A, <). In order to show that Max(L) is also regular, we can equivalently
show that L \ Max(L) is regular. Let A = (Q, i, F, A, ) be a deterministic finite au-
tomaton accepting L. Consider now the following non-deterministic finite automaton:
B = (Q × Q × {e, }, (i, i, e), F × F × {}, A, R), where the transition relation R contains
the following transitions:

       · (p, q, e) -a ((p, a), (q, a), e) for all p, q  Q and a  A;
       · (p, q, e) -a ((p, a), (q, b), ) for all p, q  Q and a, b  A with a < b;

B accepts exactly the words in L \ Max(L).

of w, i.e., w = xjyjms, then the suffix s is such that s  LU , |s| = |zj| and s lex zj. In
this case, the word w is accepted by first following the path labeled by xjyjm from (j, 0) to

(j, |xj|), then by taking the  transition from (j, |xj|) to the initial state of Sj, and then

following the unique path labeled by s in Sj. Since Sj accepts s by definition, this shows
that w is accepted by A from (j, 0). Now suppose that w = pas, repU (U|w| - 1) = pbs with
|p| < |xjyjm|, a, b  AU , a < b. Then there is a path reading pa from (j, 0) to (k, 0) where

k = (|w| - |pa|) mod d = |s| mod d. By induction hypothesis, the suffix s is accepted from

(k, 0), hence w is accepted by A from (j, 0). Moreover, Theorem 5 also implies that w does

not belong to K1 nor K2.

   We now turn to the converse inclusion. Let w  L(A) \ (K1  K2). Then no suffix of w
belongs to K1  K2 either. Again, we proceed by induction on the length of the words. By
construction of the automaton A, the word w must be accepted from the state (j, 0) where

j = |w| mod d. If |w| < n, then w  LU since w / K1. Now, suppose that w is an accepted

word of length |w|  n, and that all shorter words accepted by A but not belonging to K1

nor K2 belong to LU . Since |w|  n, the lexicographically greatest word in LU of length |w|
is repU (U|w| - 1) = xjyjmzj with j = |w| mod d and m = (|w| - |xjzj|)/d. Let us compare
w and repU (U|w| - 1).

   If these two words first differ in the prefix of length |xjyjm|, then by construction of A,
the first differing letter in w must be less than the corresponding letter in repU (U|w| - 1),
i.e., w = pas, repU (U|w| - 1) = pbs, |p| < |xjyjm|, a, b  AU , a < b. Our accepting

Since p2bs is a suffix of repU (U|w| - 1), it satisfies p2bs lex repU (U|t| - 1) by Theorem 5.

Hence t lex repU (U|t| - 1). By Theorem 5 again, we obtain that w  LU .

   We are left with the case where w and repU (U|w| - 1) are either equal or differ in the last
|zj| digits. This means that w = xjyjms with |s| = |zj|. Since w / K1  K2 and |s| < n + d,

as in the previous paragraph, all suffixes t of w satisfy t lex repU (U|t| - 1), which implies

that w  LU by Theorem 5.

   Studying the regularity of the language Max(LU ) is easier than that of LU itself since
Max(LU ) is a thin language, that is, it contains at most one word of each length [31]. This
allows us to use Theorem 6.

   We introduce one last straightforward lemma, which will allow us to separate the study
of the regularity of Max(LU ) according to the residue class modulo p for some suitable p.

Lemma 9. Let L be a language over a finite alphabet A and let p, N  N with p  1. The
language L is regular if and only if the p languages

                                  {w  L : |w|  i (mod p), |w|  N }

are all regular.

    5. Third step: Emergence of alternate bases associated with regular
                                              numeration systems

   Alternate bases are particular Cantor real bases that were independently introduced
in [10, 12]. As it turns out, the first appearance of these alternating systems of real bases
which gave rise to the study [12] is due to the observations reported in this section. See
[11] for a survey on alternate bases.

   In view of Theorem 10, with a positional numeration system with a regular language can
be associated a p-tuple of real numbers greater than or equal to 1, which correspond to the
p values of the limits. We will see that these p values play a crucial role in our study. This
will be done through the introduction of a new way of representing real numbers by using
these p values in an alternating manner. Note that non-minimal choices of p only lead us to
consider multiples of the minimal possible one, which amounts to repeating the associated
tuple of real numbers. Even though this is not forbidden as it won't be a problem of any
kind for our future developments, it does not bring any interesting feature either. So, in
what follows, we will always assume that p is minimal.

Definition 13. An alternate real base is given by a tuple B = (0, . . . , p-1) of real numbers
greater than or equal to 1. In this system, the B-value of an infinite word a = a0a1 · · ·  NN

number x. Unless we are in the degenerate case where p = 1 and 0 = 1, we can use a
greedy algorithm to find a specific B-representation of a real number x  [0, 1], which will

be called the B-expansion of x. We set r0 := x. Then, for n  N, we compute an := nrn
and rn+1 := nrn - nrn. The sequence a0a1a2 · · · of greedy digits is denoted by dB(1).
It is easily checked that this is indeed a B-representation of x. Whenever B = (0) = (1),
the greedy algorithm works only for x  {0, 1}, in which case we set dB(1) := 10.

   Among these expansions, we will be mostly interested in the expansion of 1, not only
in the base B but also in all the bases obtained as circular permutations of B. For B =
(0, . . . , p-1) and i  {0, . . . , p - 1}, we let

                      6. The quasi-greedy algorithm seen in a graph

   The quasi-greedy algorithm will be central in our study. We dedicate some notation to it.
From the recursive definition of di , we will be lead to combine the expansions with respect
to the p circular shifts of the alternate base B in order to be able to compute a quasi-greedy
expansion. In order to emphasize these links between the different shifted bases, we define
a directed graph G in the following way. The set of vertices of G is {0, . . . , p - 1}. There is
an edge going from i to (i + i) mod p if di is finite of length i. This defines a graph where
each vertex has outdegree at most 1. Whenever it exists, we let (i) denote the successor
of i, i.e.,

                                            (i) := (i + i) mod p.

This allows us to separate the vertices of G into four categories:

    (1) Vertices i with no successor.
    (2) Vertices i leading to a vertex with no successor, i.e., such that there exists r  1

          such that r(i) has no successor.
    (3) Vertices i within a cycle, i.e., such that there exists r  1 with r(i) = i.
    (4) Vertices i leading to a cycle, i.e., such that there exists r  1 such that r(i) belongs

          to a cycle.

Each of these categories will be treated separately in the proof of our main result.
   The digits of the greedy expansions will be denoted by ti,n for n  0, i.e.,

                                               di := ti,0ti,1ti,2 · · ·
     NUMERATION SYSTEMS WITHOUT A DOMINANT ROOT AND REGULARITY                          15

Moreover, we introduce the following notation to designate the prefix of di before encoun-
tering the next quasi-greedy expansion in the quasi-greedy process:

                                      di = ti,0ti,1 · · · ti,i-2(ti,i-1 - 1)

whenever di = ti,0ti,1 · · · ti,i-10 with ti,i-1 > 1. In this case, we will always keep the
notation i to refer to the length of di, i.e., the length of its prefix up to the last non-zero
digit, which we denote by

                                             di = ti,0ti,1 · · · ti,i-1.

Thus, in this situation, we have
                                                  di = didi+i .

Note that we use bold letters to designate infinite words while we use a normal font for
finite words. In particular, to avoid any confusion, we always write tails of zeros explicitly
in infinite words.

   In order to iterate the quasi-greedy process, we define

     ki,j := i + (i) + 2(i) + . . . + j-1(i)

and

                                   wi,j  :=  di di +ki,1  ·  ·  ·  d           di+ki,j  (6.1)

                                                                     i+ki,j-1

for j  0, provided that all the involved lengths are finite. In particular, note that

     · ki,0 = 0 and ki,1 = i

     · di = wi,0
     · if i leads to a vertex with no successor or itself has no successor in G, then di = wi,s

       where s  0 is such that s(i) has no successor in G.

     · if i leads to a cycle or itself belongs to a cycle in G, then wi,j is defined for all j  0
       and di = limj wi,j = didi+ki,1 · · · .

All the other words wi,j are called intermediate B(i)-expansions of 1 as they evaluate to
1 in base B(i) and they are lexicographically in between the quasi-greedy and the greedy
B(i)-expansions of 1.

   Since indices of the words di and di can be taken modulo p, we can rewrite (6.1) as

                                   wi,j := did(i) · · · dj-1(i)dj(i).                   (6.2)

Depending on the situation, we will allow ourselves to select the most convenient notation
between (6.1) or (6.2). For our further developments, we also define the values mi,j by

                                         j(i) = i + ki,j - mi,jp.                       (6.3)

                 7. Fourth step: Restriction to Parry alternate bases

   The next result is one of the key arguments of our proof. It connects the lexicographically
maximal words of each length in the numeration language to the representations of 1 in the
associated alternate base.

   We introduce the following notation, which will allow us to include alternate bases
(0, . . . , p-1) with some i equal to 1. As previously discussed, such alternate bases can
be linked to certain linear numeration systems, and therefore must be taken into account
in our study.
    NUMERATION SYSTEMS WITHOUT A DOMINANT ROOT AND REGULARITY                                              17

Definition 17. Let U be a positional numeration system with an associated alternate base
(0, . . . , p-1). Then for integers i, c, n such that 0  i < p, n  1 and 1  c  Unp-i, we
define

                                       repi,c(n) := 0repU (Unp-i - c),

where  = np - i - |repU (Unp-i - c)|.

   The idea is that we pad the greedy representation of Unp-i - c with leading zeros in order
to obtain a representation of length np - i. Most of the time, this consists in doing nothing
since if i > 1, then repi,c(n) = repU (Unp-i - c) for all large enough n. Moreover, we have
repi,1(n) = repU (Unp-i - 1) for all n  1. However, in the case where i = 1 and c  2,
these few leading zeros will ensure that we keep working with words of the desired length
np - i.

Proposition 18. Let U be a positional numeration system with an associated alternate

base (0, . . . , p-1), let i  {0, . . . , p - 1} and let c be a positive integer. For all L  0,
